opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for us the turning point is really about what changes for the person on the other side of the model. For a long time, computational tools in drug discovery were useful, but they sat at the edges. They helped you prioritize, filter, maybe rescue a campaign that was going sideways. The core work of finding a molecule that binds a target and behaves the way you want was still mostly experimental: big libraries, a lot of screening, a lot of waiting, and a lot of luck.

With Chai 2, the shift we're excited about is moving from "the model helps you search" to "the model proposes designs you actually go and test." Once your hit rates get high enough, the whole workflow inverts. You're not screening thousands or millions of things to find a handful of binders. You're designing a small set, sending them to the lab, and expecting a meaningful fraction to work. That changes timelines, cost, and which targets are even worth attempting.

From a product perspective, that's the threshold that matters. A scientist doesn't care whether a model is a few points better on a benchmark. They care whether they can take something off the screen, put it in a well, and have it work often enough to trust the process. When you cross that line, it stops being a research curiosity and becomes something people build programs around.

It also changes who can do this work. If you don't need a massive screening infrastructure to get started, a much smaller team can go after hard targets. That's a big part of why we see it as a platform shift and not just a better model.

To be clear, binding is only the first step. Developability, specificity, safety, and everything downstream still have to be earned. But getting reliable, designable binders up front is the bottleneck that's held a lot of this back, so that's the piece we think really opens things up.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll pick the answer back up from a different angle rather than continuing that line.

What makes Chai 2 feel like an inflection point to me is mostly about where the work sits. The interesting question for a product person was never raw accuracy on a benchmark. It was whether a team could plan around the output. Once you can hand someone a small set of candidates and they can budget real lab time against them, the tool stops being a curiosity and starts being part of the pipeline.

That shift changes who the customer is inside an organization. Earlier on you were selling to the person who likes trying new methods, the one with slack in their schedule to chase something speculative. Afterward you're selling to whoever owns a program timeline. Those are very different buyers with very different tolerance for surprise, and the second group asks much harder questions about reproducibility and support.

It also changed what we had to build around the model. Weights alone are not a product. People needed ways to track what they had tried, to compare runs, to explain a decision to a colleague six months later. A lot of our effort went into that scaffolding rather than the science, which surprised me at first and then stopped surprising me.

The last piece is cultural. Teams started designing experiments with the assumption that computational proposals come first and the bench confirms them, instead of the other way around. That reordering is subtle but it propagates through hiring, budgets, and how a program gets staffed. You can't really undo it once people have internalized it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making the model part of a product and pipeline, but does not say that inbound interest from pharmaceutical and biotech companies prompted that decision.

astra-6.text: I think the turning point is when the model becomes useful enough that you can build the product around it. There’s a big difference between getting an impressive response once and giving someone an experience they want to come back to. From a product perspective, that’s how I’d frame Chai 2: does it make the core experience consistently valuable? Because that’s what lets you move from demonstrating a capability to building something people actually use.

That’s the lens I’d use for Chai 2—how much closer it gets us to that kind of practical utility.
